pieces.title: PM Part 1: a weird idea with nerdy roots

script.text: What if you could buy a ticket that says it will snow in New York on Christmas? It costs 30 cents, and that price is secretly a forecast.

This is a prediction market. Instead of betting on a team, you trade a contract on whether something will happen. Will the Fed cut rates? If you're right, it pays one dollar. If you're wrong, it pays zero.
Pause and guess: if yes costs 30 cents, what is the crowd saying? About a 30 percent chance. The price is the probability.

Economists loved this for decades. Since 1988, the University of Iowa has run small real-money election markets. In one long study, they beat the polls about three times out of four. Money on the line makes people think harder.
But in America, it sat in a legal gray zone. Was it gambling, or financial trading? And the fight over that question is where this story explodes.
So next time you see a price on the future, read it as a percentage. Please follow and share for more interesting, random content like this.

pieces.caption:
A 30¢ ticket that's secretly a weather forecast.

Prediction markets let you trade on whether something will happen: a Fed rate cut, snow on Christmas, an election. Each contract pays $1 if you're right and $0 if you're wrong, so the price is the crowd's guess at the odds. 30¢ is about 30%.

Economists loved the idea for decades. The University of Iowa's small real-money election markets beat the polls about 3 times out of 4. But in the US, nobody could agree if it was gambling or trading. Part 2: how that fight turned into billions.

pieces.title: PM Part 2: the slow road vs the fast road

script.text: Two founders stared at the same legal gray zone and made opposite bets.
Kalshi's founders met at MIT and took the slow road. They spent years asking for permission, and in 2020, the CFTC approved Kalshi as a regulated exchange.
Polymarket's Shayne Coplan took the fast road: crypto, no license. Pause and guess: what happened in 2022? Regulators fined Polymarket 1.4 million dollars and made it block American users.
Then Kalshi wanted election markets. The regulator said no, so Kalshi sued, and won, about a month before the 2024 election.
Meanwhile, over 3 billion dollars was bet on Polymarket's presidential race, and one trader walked away with about 85 million. Both roads led to the same place: the mainstream.
Slow road or fast road, which would you pick? Please follow and share for more interesting, random content like this.

pieces.caption:
Two startups. Same legal gray zone. Opposite bets.

Kalshi spent years getting permission and became a regulated US exchange in 2020. Polymarket launched on crypto with no license, got fined $1.4M in 2022, and had to block American users. Then Kalshi sued its own regulator over election markets and won just before the 2024 election, while over $3B was bet on Polymarket's presidential race.
